title: Hannah Shared Her Husband With a Woman Who Tormented Her for Being Infertile
paragraphs: Hannah Shared Her Husband With a Woman Who Tormented Her for Being Infertile

She went to worship carrying an empty womb, a wounded heart, and the voice of another woman reminding her of what she could not produce. But the woman who walked into the house of God weeping would eventually walk into history carrying a testimony—and her story whispers something breathtaking about Jesus: your most painful chapter does not get to write your ending.
Imagine sitting at your own family table and watching another woman’s children gather around the man you love.
Imagine hearing their laughter.
Watching him hand portions of food to them.
Seeing everything you desperately prayed for living right in front of you—but belonging to someone else.
And then imagine the mother of those children knowing exactly where your deepest wound was...
and deliberately pressing it.
Again.
And again.
And again.
That is where Hannah’s story begins.
Not with Samuel.
Not with answered prayer.
Not with victory.
With humiliation.
Scripture introduces the household almost brutally:
Elkanah “had two wives: the name of one was Hannah and the name of the other Peninnah; and Peninnah had children, but Hannah had no children” (1 Samuel 1:2).
One sentence.
Two women.
One husband.
And one devastating contrast.
Peninnah had children.
Hannah did not.

We should be careful here because biblical accuracy matters more than a dramatic headline. Scripture does not tell us that Hannah personally chose Peninnah, invited her into the marriage, or willingly arranged to share Elkanah with another woman. It tells us simply that Elkanah had two wives.
And the Bible recording polygamy is not the Bible endorsing it.
Jesus later pointed marriage back to the creation pattern: “the two shall become one flesh” (Matthew 19:4–6; compare Genesis 2:24).
The fractured household in 1 Samuel shows us exactly what so many Old Testament households show us: human arrangements can create devastating rivalries, jealousy, comparison and pain.
Hannah was living inside one of them.
And what makes her story especially painful is that Elkanah loved her.
Love did not remove the ache.
Every year the family traveled to Shiloh to worship and sacrifice to the LORD.
Peninnah had sons and daughters.
Hannah had none.
Elkanah gave Hannah a special portion because he loved her.
But there are wounds even sincere human love cannot heal.
A husband can hold you and still not be able to fix what is breaking inside you.
A friend can tell you everything will be okay and still not understand why you cry when nobody is watching.
People can genuinely love you...
and still be powerless to give you the thing your heart has been begging God for.
Then Scripture introduces the cruelty.
The Hebrew of 1 Samuel 1:6 calls Peninnah:
צָרָתָהּ — ṣārātāh
Her rival. Her adversary.
And the verse describes her provoking Hannah severely in order to distress her because Hannah’s womb was closed.
The language matters.
This was not an innocent misunderstanding.
This was not Hannah simply being overly sensitive.
Peninnah knew where the wound was.
And she touched it deliberately.
The Hebrew uses language associated with vexation, grief, agitation and provocation.
Then comes one of the saddest details:
שָׁנָה בְשָׁנָה — shanah veshanah.
“Year by year.”
This was not one terrible afternoon.
It became a pattern.
Year after year.
Journey after journey.
Worship after worship.
Hannah went toward the house of God while somebody beside her kept reopening the same wound.
Eventually she wept.
She could not eat.
Maybe that sentence feels uncomfortably familiar.
Because perhaps your Peninnah is not a woman.
Maybe your Peninnah is the pregnancy announcement you smiled at before going into another room and crying.
Maybe it is watching someone else get married while you quietly wonder whether anybody will ever choose you.
Maybe it is seeing someone younger receive the opportunity you prayed for.
Maybe it is scrolling through photographs of happy families while yours is falling apart.
Maybe it is watching somebody celebrate the healing you still have not received.
Maybe it is another rejection email.
Another negative test.
Another funeral.
Another relapse.
Another birthday with the same unanswered prayer.
Another Sunday where everybody around you seems to be singing about God’s goodness while you are wondering why His goodness feels so difficult to see from where you are sitting.
There are pains that become harder because somebody else possesses what you lack.
And comparison knows how to turn another person’s blessing into evidence against God's love.
“If God loves me, why them and not me?”
“If God hears prayer, why am I still waiting?”
“What is wrong with me?”
“Did I do something to deserve this?”
“Has God forgotten me?”
Hannah's story refuses to give shallow answers to those questions.
Scripture does something startling.
It says the LORD had closed her womb.
That statement should make us careful, not careless.

It does not give Christians permission to look at every infertile woman, every sick person, every tragedy, every disability, every delayed prayer and announce that we know exactly why God permitted it.
We do not.
Jesus Himself rejected simplistic equations between individual suffering and personal sin (John 9:1–3).
Hannah's particular story tells us what happened in Hannah's particular story.
And we know something Hannah did not yet know.
Her closed womb was not the conclusion.
But she had to live inside the sentence before she could see the next paragraph.
That may be where some people reading this are right now.
You believe God writes stories.
You simply hate the paragraph you are currently living in.
Then Elkanah asks her:
“Hannah, why do you weep? Why do you not eat? Why is your heart sad?”
He loved her.
But love does not always equal understanding.
Then he asks, in essence, “Am I not better to you than ten sons?”
Perhaps he meant comfort.
But Hannah needed more than distraction from her longing.
She needed God.
So Hannah got up.
Do not rush past that.
She got up.
Still barren.
Still hurting.
Still misunderstood.
Still carrying an unanswered prayer.
She got up.
Some victories begin before circumstances change.
Sometimes faith looks spectacular.
Sometimes faith looks like a wounded person getting up from the table.
Hannah went before the LORD.
And Scripture says:
וְהִיא מָרַת נָפֶשׁ — vehi marat nafesh.
She was “bitter of soul,” deeply distressed.
She prayed.
And she wept bitterly.
This is one of the reasons Hannah's story remains so powerful thousands of years later.
She did not clean herself up emotionally before approaching God.
She did not pretend everything was fine.
She did not manufacture a religious smile.
She brought God the wound.
There is a kind of prayer that sounds beautiful in church.
And then there is the prayer you pray when beautiful sentences have abandoned you.
Hannah prayed that prayer.
Her lips moved.
Her voice could not be heard.
Eli the priest watched her and assumed she was drunk.
Think about that.
Peninnah misunderstood her pain.
Her husband could not solve her pain.
And now even the priest misunderstood her prayer.
Have you ever been hurting so deeply that even the people who were supposed to understand you got you wrong?
Hannah answers Eli:
“No, my lord, I am a woman troubled in spirit... I have been pouring out my soul before the LORD” (1 Samuel 1:15).
Pouring.
Not presenting.
Not performing.
Pouring.
There is a difference.
Some of us have spent years presenting ourselves to God when He has been waiting for us to pour ourselves out before Him.
The anger.
The jealousy you are ashamed to admit.
The exhaustion.
The questions.
The grief.
The disappointment.
The secret resentment.
The fear that everybody else's life is moving while yours remains frozen.
Bring it.
God is not intimidated by the prayer you are afraid to say.
Hannah vowed that if God gave her a son, she would give that son back to the LORD.
And eventually Scripture says something extraordinarily tender:
“The LORD remembered her” (1 Samuel 1:19).
That does not mean God had previously forgotten Hannah and suddenly remembered she existed.
Biblically, God's “remembering” frequently signals His movement in covenant faithfulness toward someone or something already known to Him.
Hannah conceived.
She gave birth.
And she named the child Samuel.
But here is where the story becomes far bigger than “a woman prayed for a baby and finally got one.”
Because Samuel was not merely Hannah's answer.
Samuel would become one of Israel's great prophetic figures.
He would minister before the LORD.
He would speak God's word.
He would participate in one of the great transitions in Israel's history.
And eventually Samuel would anoint a young shepherd named David.
David.
The king to whom God would give covenant promises.
The royal line that the New Testament ultimately connects to Jesus Christ.
Do you see the breathtaking sweep?
Hannah was crying over a womb.
God was moving history toward a kingdom.
Hannah could see her humiliation.
God could see generations.
She could see Peninnah.
God could see Samuel.
She could see an empty cradle.
God could see a prophet.
She could see today's agony.
God's redemptive purposes stretched far beyond what she could see.
But we must not turn Hannah's story into a formula.
“Pray hard enough and God will give you a baby.”
No.
That is not the Gospel.
Some faithful women pray for children and never conceive.
Some faithful believers die waiting for prayers whose answers they never see in this life.
Some marriages are not restored.
Some bodies are not healed before resurrection.
Some graves remain occupied.
Christian hope cannot depend on receiving Hannah's exact earthly outcome.
It depends on receiving Hannah's God.
And ultimately...
on Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest human problem is greater than infertility, loneliness, rejection, poverty, sickness or disappointment.
Our deepest problem is sin.
We are separated from the holy God who made us, and no amount of earthly success can repair that separation.
We do not merely need improved circumstances.
We need reconciliation.
We need forgiveness.
We need redemption.
We need a Savior.
And Jesus Christ came.
The Son of God entered our broken world.
He lived the righteousness we could never produce.
He carried our sin to the cross.
He was rejected.
Mocked.
Wounded.
Crucified.
And the apparent scandal of the cross became the place where grace was displayed.
Christ died for sinners.
And on the third day...
the grave lost its claim.
Jesus rose.
That is why Christianity offers something stronger than “your difficult season will eventually improve.”
Sometimes it will.
Sometimes it will not.
The Gospel offers something infinitely greater:
In Christ, suffering does not have the final word.
Sin does not have the final word.
Shame does not have the final word.
Your past does not have the final word.
Even death does not have the final word.
Jesus does.
Maybe that is why you needed Hannah's story today.
Not because God is promising to give you exactly what He gave Hannah.
But because the God Hannah cried to is still worthy of being trusted when you cannot see what He is doing.
Maybe you have been secretly angry with Him.
Tell Him.
Maybe you stopped praying because unanswered prayer became too painful.
Come back.
Maybe comparison has poisoned your ability to celebrate anybody else's blessing.
Confess it.
Maybe you are smiling publicly while privately becoming bitter.
Pour it out.
Maybe you have been running from Christ because shame convinced you that you needed to become better before coming home.
You don't clean yourself before coming to the One who cleanses sinners.
Come to Jesus.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the thing that is killing you and into the mercy Christ purchased with His blood.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace brings us home and begins transforming us.
And maybe your prayer tonight does not need to be impressive.
Maybe it only needs to be true.
“Jesus, I need You.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I am angry.”
“Jesus, I am tired.”
“Jesus, I don't understand.”
“Jesus, help me trust You.”
You do not have to explain the whole story.
Two words are enough.
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not the only Christian who loves Jesus and still cries.
Someone may pray for you.
Someone may finally become honest because you became honest first.
Someone currently standing where you once stood may desperately need evidence that Christians can hurt deeply without being abandoned by Christ.
Then think of one person whose private battle you know.
Not twenty random people.
One person.
The woman struggling to conceive.
The man whose marriage is collapsing.
The believer who has become spiritually exhausted.
The friend who quietly stopped attending church.
The person who still believes in God but no longer knows how to talk to Him.
Not merely to increase numbers.
They may be surrounded by people and still feel unbearably alone.
They may never tell you what they are carrying.
One share can put biblical truth in front of somebody you never knew needed it.
Because today's encouragement can become tomorrow night's lifeline.

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even the person who does not yet believe—to follow with you for daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.

Supporting Gospel ministry is not a way to purchase God's favor, earn salvation, prove that you glorify God, or force Him to bless you. Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ, not a transaction.
But Christians can glorify God by freely and cheerfully supporting faithful Gospel work and helping biblical truth reach others.
And there is already an enormous amount you can access freely.
Come to Jesus.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not merchandise.
Jesus.
Because Hannah's greatest legacy is not that she finally received what she wanted.
It is that her suffering drove her to pour herself before God.
And when Samuel finally came, she understood that even the answer belonged to Him.
That is surrender.
Perhaps the miracle you need most is not simply God changing what is around you.
Perhaps it is Christ transforming what is within you while you wait.
So tonight, when everybody else has gone quiet...
when the announcements stop...
when the photographs disappear...
when you are alone again with the thing you cannot fix...
remember Hannah.
She cried.
She hurt.
She was misunderstood.
She was provoked year after year.
She carried a prayer nobody around her could answer.
But her tears were not invisible to God.
And neither are yours.
We cannot promise that your story will end with Hannah's exact miracle.
We can promise something Scripture gives every person who belongs to Christ:
your story does not end at the grave.
There is resurrection coming.
There is restoration coming.
There is a day when Christ will make all things new.
So repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Stop pretending where you need to become honest.
Pray again.
Open Scripture again.
Come home again.
Trust Jesus again.
And if all you can manage tonight is a trembling whisper...
let His name be the whisper.
Jesus.
Because perhaps the sentence you thought destroyed your story...
was only the place where you stopped writing and finally placed the pen into God's hands.
Your wound may explain one chapter—but only Jesus has the authority to write the final sentence.
